p: Approximately, I believe 82,000.
Thank you and you said 55 to -

About 55 to 60 percent each week are showing up to their appointments and for cash assistance, we have an ongoing and expansive engagement process where for individuals who did not show up, we have a process to engage them and follow the cash assistance conciliation and sanction process, which happens over several weeks.
Okay, great uhm, can you walk us through the CBO partnership pathways and how many CBO’S have applied to become partners with HRA?

Sure, so uh I’m happy to say and also very thankful to the CBO community that over 100 CBO’s have stepped forward and that number actually increases each week. It is an open enrollment, so there is no deadline. Uh, as CBO’s learn about it, we’re determined it is something they think they might be able to do. We welcome them to submit the

form. And then based upon the activities the CBO’s have, uhm, and you know what capacity they have to support, they will either be put into one of the two pathways you had talked about. One of the pathways has a little bit more administrative support that is being brought where those organizations will a., receive referrals directly from us as well as help track compliance and hours and report that in to us. Uh, on the other pathway, that is more of a connection made between the individual and the organization. Most likely an organization that are already connected to. They may attend programming or receive other case management services where they can access volunteer opportunities and then submit to us on a monthly basis, right uh compliance with those volunteer hours.

Great thank you. Okay, we know that the agency has been warning people who are meeting ABAWD work requirements but the agency will not begin to take negative action until June 2026. Does DSS have an estimate on how many SNAP clients may lose SNAP benefits during the first month when the agency will begin to take action for noncompliance?

Uh, we do not have that estimate at the time. We’re going to be tracking closely each month to see how many individuals are actually coming close to the three months. Uhm, cause that will really then give us a sense of how many people may be impacted. We’ll also be able to really target our outreach and engagement closely because we’ll be able to target specifically the people we know who maybe have had two months of noncompliance. So, that - the third month is really essential. So, we’re happy to keep the Council updated as we see that - the first - the first data that we’ll have will be in the very beginning of April when we see what happened in the month of March.

Okay, thank you. With the reinstitution of work requirements for cash assistance clients, we know HRA has been projecting an increase in the demand for childcare vouchers for those who are on cash assistance. As of the recent PMMR in the first four months of Fiscal 2026, around 596,000 individuals in New York City are on both SNAP and cash assistance. This roughly represents one third of the total SNAP population. How many HRA

Cash Assistance Childcare Vouchers have been issued this month?

Uhm, I will have to get back to you on the monthly. I can say as of right now, there are 30,000 households currently receiving childcare vouchers through HRA uhm as part of compliance with cash assistance mandatory engagement.
Okay, so uhm, maybe you’ll have to get back to me on this one as well then. How many of the vouchers were issued to clients on both SNAP and Cash Assistance?

I’ll have to get back to you on that. I will just clarify, the requirement for childcare on the HRA side is connected specifically to Cash Assistance requirements. There is not mandated childcare required on SNAP for individuals on ABAWD. They would be exempted having children under the age of 14 and on the cash side, childcare is required for individuals under who have a child under the age of 14 in the household.

Okay. Uhm, we know HRA has been rolling out the resumption of work requirements and phases over time. How much growth have you seen uh since in cash assistance childcare vouchers since

this began and how does it compare to the level of vouchers seen prior to pandemic?

Uhm, I’ll get back to you on the level of growth. It is lower than prepandemic because we have been slowly rolling out mandatory engagement and we hadn’t uhm actually had mandatory engagement in place for many years during the uh pandemic. We only rolled out mandatory engagement again last April of 2025 and we’ve been taking it in a very methodical way but we can get back to you on the trends that you asked about.
Okay, that would be great. And does HRA anticipate needing more staffing to handle the Administration for the projected increase and demand for cash assistance childcare vouchers?
No, at this point, we believe we have appropriate staffing to support that.
Okay, great. Uhm, I’m going to pause here and turn it over to some of my colleagues. Uhm, starting with Council Member Morano.

Thank you Chair. Commissioner Dalton, thank you for your testimony. Congratulations on your new role and good luck. You,

in your testimony outlined billions in spending and tens of thousands of placements. The shelter census as you pointed out is still over 85,000 people. At what point do we say the current model isn’t reducing homelessness and just managing it and is there anything we as policy makers could be doing to more effectively get people out of the - I don’t know the shelter pipeline?

I’ll start uhm and then turn it over to my colleagues who will probably have a more informed answer but I think it’s - it’s a great question and something I want to understand better. With so many additional exits from the shelter system and perhaps fewer new entrance from asylees, I would expect to start to see declines in the shelter population. It’s something you know in my first few weeks, I want to take a really good look at. I think uhm, I think what we want to do is be moving people into shelter who need it of course and then moving them onto permanent housing as quickly as possible. And so, I think it’s worth a really good look but uhm, if the Administrator Fellini wanted to add anything, please feel free.

Thank you Commissioner. I would echo your sentiments, that we’re looking to uhm, ensure that we’re meeting the needs of those who are coming in and moving them to permanent housing as quickly as possible.

Commissioner, you stated that roughly 98 percent of spending goes to direct benefits. Does that include shelter costs, administrative overhead embedded in contracts and hotel placements? I’m wondering if you can clearly define what counts as a direct benefit to a taxpayer?

I will turn that over because I certainly don’t know the details of the contracts to nonprofits in particular or to hotels but I think uhm, you do see a very low administrative rate in HRA and DHS. I think the numbers I cited were 4 percent and 3 percent. So, those being low administrative rates, with the vast, vast majority of those dollars going directly to New Yorkers but let me - let me get my colleague.

Yeah, so they uhm, the direct benefits there would include things like public assistance or Medicaid, SNAP, uhm, and the entitlement programs that uh the DSS collectively

administers. It would not include uhm, uh, the shelter costs that you noted.

One final question if I may. Uhm, you’re expanding low barrier beds and shelter capacity. What specific steps are you taking to reduce demand so communities are continuously asked to absorb new facilities? I especially ask because in my district in Staten Island, there are plans for a new facility there.

Again, I’ll start and then turn it over. Uhm, I think it’s a great opportunity to talk about our Homebase program, which helps to prevent homelessness and I’ll let my colleagues do that. I think that program has been effective and I think just like you said, we want to be moving people as quickly as we can into permanent housing. And so, uhm, the other thing I would just say is all of the other benefits that DSS, HRA offer, are the kinds of things that prevent homelessness in the first place right? We want to be able to provide every dollar that New Yorkers are eligible to receive and with those dollars, they don’t have to make you know choices between healthcare or childcare and housing. And so, making sure we really maximize and do what we

can particularly during this time of HR1 to keep dollars in the hands of eligible New Yorkers, will hopefully also reduce homelessness but maybe an opportunity to talk about Homebase a little bit.

Sure I can take the Homebase question. Uhm, so yeah, so the Homebase program has proven to be very successful in diverting people from shelter. You know every year, it’s about 95 percent of those who engage with Homebase do not enter shelter. Uh, last year they served approximately 32,000. Uhm, you know we are definitely looking at uh ways in which some of the activities Homebase currently does with uhm households to bring some of those in - back into HRA, right? Homebase is definitely taking on a lot of work around subsidies and subsidy uh management and some other complex cases that we’ve created a new unit in HRA so that we can handle more complex cases and they can serve more people in the community. And so, we’re finalizing some of those plans so that that will continue to increase Homebase’s capacity to serve people you know in community and divert them from shelter.
And let me also ask my colleague at DHS to talk about the diversion programs we have there as well.

Thank you Commissioner, Administrator and Council Member for the question. Uhm, our approach at DHS always is to explore all diversion options, right? So, if somebody comes to us, they’re in a housing crisis. They’re in an emergency situation. So, we first want to understand what that is and what options they have. The first step is not always placement into shelter, it’s to explore all options.
Thanks very much.
Thank you Council Member. I’d like to uhm announce that we’ve been joined by Council Member Nurse as well and turning it over to Council Member Sanchez.

Thank you so much Madam Chair and good morning. Congratulations Commissioner on your appointment. I look forward to working with you. Uhm, I want to just ask a few questions about City FHEPS. Uhm, City FHEPS is one of the most effective tools that our city has to stabilize families, which is why this Council passed and then

overroad the previous Mayor’s veto to expand eligibility of the program. Uhm, even as those conversations continue between the Administration, Mayor Mamdani committed as a candidate to uh, to release - uh I don’t know that’s not the right word but to let go of that lawsuit uhm and I want to you know just park that conversation except to say that that is a - the bills that we pass and the expansion that we legislated is very important to this Council and I want to make sure that we are honoring the original intent of that legislation. But even with that aside, uhm, you know this - this budget - the Mayor has and the agency has increased funding for the existing program, $711 million more in ‘26, $1.64 billion more in ‘27 uhm, growing to $2.6 billion in 2030 for the City FHEPs program. Can you help us understand uh what - what - just break down the cost of this program for us. What rent levels has the city seen most commonly used with a voucher? Can you follow up with a chart and just data that can help us understand what rents we’re covering, what rent levels we’re covering? And uh, can you help us understand the cost drivers? Thank you.

Yeah, thank you for that question. I can take that. Uhm, so in the latest PMMR, we reported that the average subsidy for City FHEPS is $1,908. Uhm, this is a newly released statistic. Uhm, generally speaking for City FHEPs, uhm just like any other rental assistance program, the cost drivers for the program are the number of individuals that are entering the program, you know, the number of individuals that are leaving the program and how long they stay within that program. There’s also a component that uhm is rent as you’ve noted and there we follow the payment standard as set by the New York City Housing Authority.
So, what are we seeing? What are we seeing in terms of number of individuals entering, leaving and staying, lengths of stay? I’m sorry Chair.
Oh yes, I’m sorry. So, uhm, the program in total enrolls about 68,000. So, what I have here are the new enrollments for uh Fiscal Year ‘25, which was about 15,000 new enrollees over that fiscal year.
And how does that trend uhm, what are we projecting?
Uhm, that is a pretty consistent number. So, we are projecting the growth to stay fairly consistent over the uhm, over the period of the plan.
So, 68,000 people per year, families per year?
No, no, I’m sorry, 15,000 new families per year.
New, and how long are people staying enrolled?
Uhm, you know that I don’t actually have available but we can get back to you with that number.

Okay, thank you. Just to say that the Council has for many years uhm, been asking many questions about the cost drivers and lengths of stay, rent levels and all of that. Happy to see the new statistic in the PMMR but we want to be a partner in understanding what the cost drivers are and identifying solutions to contain the cost, so that we can reach more families. Thank you Chair.
Thank you so much Council Member. Uhm, Council Member Brewer followed by Council Member Nurse.

Thank you. Congratulations Commissioner. We also like Scott French very much. 24/7 calling him, two o’clock in the morning, no problem. Uhm, I have - I teach at Hunter College and this morning I was there and somebody had apparently has an idea about putting algorithms; this is about SNAP, algorithms on persons who are caught up in this Trump hell. And so you would be able to contact them more easily on their cellphone. $25 million to be saved. So, I am going to send you this proposal; another professor gave it to me. Is that something that you’re aware of? Are you using technology to help people not get caught up in Trump hell?

Uh, yes, we are using technology that I’m very interested in reading that proposal. You know in regards to communications, right, we are pushing out also you know text messages, push notifications. We’re going to be rolling out robo calls and other things directly to individuals who need to comply with the ABAWD requirements and always willing and open to look at other utilization of technology to make sure people have the information they need and we’re also making it as simple as

possible for them to report to us any information they need to so that we can ensure that they are remaining compliant and keep their SNAP benefits.
Okay.

Just one thing to add and Administrator French talked about this a little bit in some of his answers but uhm, I think it requires sort of a whole of government effort to make sure we’re a., reaching out to people and b., exempting people where we can. Most of the people on SNAP who aren’t already working, uhm, are exempt from working. And so, if we can make sure we understand their eligibility, any uhm, challenges they may have in working, we can exempt them forever and then they don’t have to - they don’t have to go through the onerous processes designed to get people off of benefits.

I know- I mean I’ve been doing this work since 1978 and since then, people don’t pay attention to anything. So, it’s uh, it’s hard. They just don’t. They are in another world, so the more that you can tell them in ten times - I just think this technology might really help.

Number two, just sweeps. I know uh, Scott knows I’m working on this a lot of encampment. People are difficult. They just like to stay out. So, I’m just wondering how many uh, encampments have you - obviously I know the Mayor had a position not uhm move them but I know that in some cases, you just have to. And again, some people just don’t want to go to an apartment. They just want to be out but my question is how many people have you moved? Were you able to get them shelter? Uhm, how are you identifying encampments? I know they’re not supposed to be called encampments but that’s what I call them. And I just want to know, just generally how you’re handling them and what the numbers are.

So, I will start and then pass to Administrator Fellini to provide some of the details. Uhm, so as you know, this Administration has asked the Department of Homeless Services to take the lead in engaging with people staying on the street, in community and in encampments, and I think that is the right move. These are - these are the outreach workers who have built trust over weeks and years and these are the people who know where the resources are and can help meet those needs. And so, as that work

continues with partners, I think for me, it’s really important to try to offer people what they want. While I agree, there are always some people, a very small number who will never come inside and some who won’t come inside on that day. If we can meet their needs, if we can make sure their belongings are kept uhm, if they can’t take them with them to the next location and if we do treat people with dignity and respect in that process, I think a lot of folks will accept those offers. And so, that was maybe enough time for the Administrator to find the numbers we have been working on so far.
Okay, thank you.

Thank you Commissioner and Council Member, yes thank you. Since January, we have conducted around 40 cleanings and have made referrals to 85 individuals into the system. I don’t know how many have actually come in but we could look into them.

Mine got swept March 11th and they’re right back this morning. Just FYI, so that’s what I’m dealing with. Just also, uhm, on the

City FHEPS, good question from my colleague but after - how much time does one have on City FHEPS and have those deadlines - I think it’s five years? And then what happens? Or maybe you haven’t hit that deadline yet in many cases.

Uh, yeah, the, the, program is a five year program, right? As long as individuals keep meeting eligibility and then after five years, uhm, we will review on a case by case basis if the subsidy would continue.

Okay and then there’s a program that we used to have where basically it was direct to housing. You know and so, I know in other places in the country, you probably know Commissioner, it exists. It was a pilot. I believe it ended. Is that something that is continuing? How much does it cost and is it effective? Because to me, it might be effective but it’s probably expensive but worth the money in my opinion.
Yeah.
Does it exist and how much it costs?

Yup, uhm, and letting my colleagues get to the place in the briefing book where they

might be able to give you numbers there too. I understand it was a pilot that is continuing actually, so we continue to work with, I think it’s Volunteers of America to place people directly from streets-
And how many people have been placed and what’s the cost?

Sure, so uhm, I’ll get back to you on the exact costs you know but people are placed uhm, utilizing uh, housing subsidies, City FHEPS, sometimes some other subsidies. Uhm, but uh we also provide a payment to uhm, support the move straight from the street into housing while we work on whatever is needed for - you know whatever applications may be needed whether it’s supportive housing or otherwise. I can say uh, the current program has 81 units and since over its inception, 151 street homeless individuals have housed uh, have utilized the program. Currently there are 64 participants in the 81 units and we have approximately 15 clients currently scheduled to view the current units uhm, after being engaged by our outreach teams and expressing interest in participating in this.
So, wouldn’t - is it successful? Is it more successful than any other way of getting people off the street or is it not clear yet?

Uh, I think it is another tool which we are always happy to have. Uhm, we are exploring the possibility of expanding it to see if there is a scale that might be able to be met by the program. That’s still under discussion so, I’m happy to continue to you know update you on that but we are always happy to have as many tools as we possibly can that may resonate with someone when another tool would not.

Okay, last question, coordination with other agencies. I’ve been to so many hearings, I can’t remember but I think it was at - maybe it was DCAS. The bottomline is when people are taking other kinds of services, in other words they could then be asked about SNAP or asked about cash assistance, whatever. Is that something - how do you coordinate that internally or if you are? In other words- people - this is a new day with you know the guy in the White House and everything else. So, my question is, how are you coordinating with other

agencies so people hear about your services. You know could be even tenant assistance etc.. My understanding is that’s something that’s somewhat new in this Administration.
And again, I’ll let my colleagues jump in here but i had a conversation with the Commissioner of health yesterday and one of his main goals -
I think it was the Commissioner who said this, yeah.
Yeah, working along side-
The guy from Harvard, yes.

Yeah, working alongside of us is yes, to take that extra step if someone is receiving WIC. If somebody is in the medical clinic, how do we ask them about their food security, connect them to SNAP? And we can do the same, right? So, we could ask if people uhm -
So, you haven’t started doing it but he is doing now, is that the idea? How - it should be on a massive scale in my opinion.
Great, every city worker who engages with people should be able to offer those opportunities and I think -
You need training- you need training. So, is that happening?

Yeah, so we currently do have you know a lot of partnerships, which we can always expand, especially with the other agencies within the Health and Human Services portfolio, DOHMH, Aging, ACS, many others. Uhm, uh, we are working closely with the Mayor’s Office of Tenant Protections and others to make sure that we are all sort of cross training and providing cross information, so that they have access to the information on our programs and vice versa uhm, but obviously very - always open to working on something that goes beyond that in scope.

Okay and NYCHA also, I’m just saying, I don’t think it happened in the past, that’s my personal experience, so it would be good to know exactly how that training is taking place and if it’s really happening and what the outcomes are. Thank you.
Thank you Council Member. Council Member Nurse.

Thank you Chair. Uhm, and just want to double down on the Street to Home pilot. It’s in my district. It’s very successful actually and hopefully there’s a way for you all to evaluate and formally say, officially say that but from my understanding in every conversation I’ve had, it’s been very successful. I think they’re looking for more referrals. So, at a more frequent rate and my understanding is there are people who have actually moved into, like fully permanent you know their permanent home that they want to be in. So, huge advocate for that. I want to talk about uhm, DHS Immigration Customs Enforcement as it relates to shelters. Uhm, Gotham had an article last - the end of last year, there were about five instances of ICE agents gaining access to DHS shelters in violation of our Sanctuary laws. Two incidents where ICE was permitted to enter a DHS facility without providing a judicial warrant. Two incidents of ICE agents and NYPD Officers entering a DHS facility without staff permission. One incident of a shelter employee providing ICE

agents with information about a former shelter resident. So, with this, what have you all done to train up your staff, make sure everyone at the front door knows what - what we should not be doing, what would be violating our city laws, uhm, are you training people in person, are you sending people out, are you doing it remote? Give us an update on how we’re remedying this situation.

Thank you for the question, Council Member. Uhm, we have had limited uhm encounters with ICE at DHS shelters. Uhm, we have taken a multipronged approach to make sure that the correct information is out there and that staff on the ground, in the middle of the night, feel supported by the agency when things do occur. So, we’ve reissued our facility access policy so that there’s formal information about what DHS’s directive is about how to handle this.
Like an email? Like an all staff email or something?

Yeah, it’s shared through the provider community. There’s an online database of policies and procedures. We send it as an

attachment. We reference it. We make sure people have copies of it. Uhm, we have also created a flow chart when a 30 page procedure does not really help. We have a flow chart that people can have at the front desk so they know exactly what the steps are when they are ensuring that non-local Law Enforcement is properly identifying themselves and demonstrating a judicial warrant. Uhm, we’ve also uhm shared a list of our on-call attorney’s, 24 hours a day 7 days a week, so people on the ground feel supported in the moment when things are happening. Uhm, and we’ve also advised staff to not engage in any altercations with any uhm, agents. We are regularly engaging with providers around this after an incident. As a reminder, we have DHS staff that are responsible for ensuring our providers are implementing policies and procedures, regularly following up and every time we hear, we reiterate and make sure that everybody understands. We’ve done in person trainings, we’ve done Zoom trainings, we’ve done big meetings.

Okay, and so, as part of what you’re talking about, in the past, you all had stated that you implemented a most robust procedure

for verifying arrest warrants after one of these incidents happen. Is this part of that process or is there anything you could tell us about the procedure change?
Apologies, I’ll have to get back to you.

Okay, yeah and for it to be specific, it was that you all had somehow helped people at the front understand how to verify an arrest warrant. So, if there’s a procedure change, please let us know. Uhm, in one incident, ICE was, ICE agents were given access to the residents sign in book. Uhm, have you done any follow up to see what names were - were uhm, they were given access to and taking any safety measures for those people?
I am not aware of that, so we’ll look into that.

Okay, uhm, I think those are all my questions. Just want to make sure we’re protecting our folks and not violating our laws. Uhm, and so, however we can be supportive of that as well, please let us know. If we can help at our district level, we will but we want to make sure

folks aren’t getting kidnapped. So, thank you so much.
Got it and if I could Council Member.
Yeah.

I just got advised, uhm, into your question about verifying arrest warrants. We’ve provided samples of the federal warrants and subpoenas, so staff know how to identify them as being the right type that we allow an agent -
Like, that’s at the front desk, like the flow chart, and those samples?
We’ll make sure.
Okay.
I believe it’s part of the procedure but we’ll make sure.
Yeah, I think that’s helpful because in the moment people panic and they forget you know where to find it. And so, just a place to reference would be helpful. Okay, thank you Chair.

Okay, thank you Council Member. I’d like to acknowledge that we’ve also been joined by Council Member Avilés.

Uhm, so I want to move uh, into a different set of questions. Uhm, I’ll be hoping around just a little bit here but uh regarding employees on benefits programs. While the people who work at DHS, HRA, and their contracted CBO’s do invaluable work serving our city’s most vulnerable, work in the provision in social services is often poorly compensated, leading to many employees relying on the same benefits they help others access. Is this something that you track and can you share the percentage of DHS, HRA, or contracted CBO employees who are receiving public benefits such as cash assistance, SNAP or housing vouchers?

Uh, I think we’ll have to get back to you on the city employees. I’m not sure that we have that data but we can check and come back to you on the CBO providers. I’m not sure how that would be possible because we don’t have the full list of -

The details, okay but is this something that you track as far as you’re aware? Do you know - I know you’ll get back to me on the specific number but do you know that you have employees that are on public assistance?
I mean, we are aware that there are employees who may be on public assistance right. Uhm, I am not aware of tracking but I don’t want to speak definitely in that statement.
Okay.
Uhm, you know we - uh but you know we are aware that there are - as you noted you know individuals who potentially are definitely accessing some of our benefits.
And do we know how many employees are in city shelters?
I don’t have that number now but yes, we know that number. We can get that to you.
Okay, great and how does DSS support its own employees who are currently enrolled in public benefits to assist them toward self sufficiency?

Uhm, we always internally right, there is very much a commitment to developing pathways of development for staff members. I will say over the last you know couple of years and we can get back to you with some more details, right? We have developed a lot of uh trainings and other sort of like engagement and academies, including an

academy for frontline workers, which recently occurred over the summer for the first time ever, which was a great thing. That is really about connecting individuals to a., what internal resources are available to help develop someone’s career. Uh, what can we connect to them externally that also is around there? So, we are having to follow up with some additional specifics around that but I will say over the last couple of years, the agency has really focused on building out uh, our staff development efforts, so that staff have places to go to explore what options are there for them to you know build their careers at HRA and also just to think long term where they may want to be going to.

That’s great. Thank you and I just want to state for the record uhm, my own advocacy for pay parity across agencies, which I’ve talked about previously as Chair of the Aging Committee where we see social workers and case workers and some agencies making less than the same roles in other agencies, which I think is a direct reflection of our values. And in that case, particularly we don’t value older adults and the work that people do around older adults. And so,

similarly, you know this is a space where frontline workers are working with vulnerable populations and they become vulnerable populations themselves. And so, anything and everything we can do to help support you and your efforts in supporting staff and employees so that they’re not also receiving public benefits, I think would be great work. Uhm, shelter costs new need. The Council has long called on the Administration to more accurately budget for the cost of DHS’s shelter system, which has been under budgeted at adoption in recent years. We were glad to see a baseline increase of city funding for shelters included in the preliminary plan. $586.1 million in Fiscal 2026, $988.6 million in Fiscal 2027, and $1.04 billion in Fiscal 2028, $1.09 billion in Fiscal 2029 and $1.15 billion in Fiscal 2030. Additionally, there are net decreases of state and federal funding. And 146 baselined positions were added starting in Fiscal 2026. Can you tell me more about how the funding amounts were determined?

Yes, thank you for that question. I’m happy to take this. So, we do coordinate very closely with the Office of Management and Budget on

our projections for the census, for utilization, length of stay in our DHS program. Uhm, and we uhm, coordinate on- on that data and how it translates into the budget. So, the dollar amounts in this most recent preliminary budget reflect what we believe will be the spending for uhm, through the five year budget period. I mean obviously projections will change but this is what we think we would spend.
And uhm, what are DHS’s projections for the shelter census in the coming years?
Thank you for the question. We work with our partners at the Office of Management and Budget on shelter projections and I do not have those numbers at this time but we can share them.
Okay and why is federal and state funding being decreased? What were the funding sources?

Uhm, yeah sorry, so that- uhm, the adjustments that you see in the budget related to federal and state are mostly just cleaning up some of the modifications and adjustments that have been made at periods before the beginning of Fiscal Year. So, those would have been all related to say TANF and

state contributions uhm, but the budget currently reflects what we believe will be the projected spending between city, federal and state funding.
Okay and what are the titles and job descriptions for the 146 additional positions?
Uhm, that piece we’ll have to get back to you on. Uhm, the information I have here is just the total. So, we’ll get back to you on what the titles are and how that dollar amount -
Okay and also, I would love to know when you plan to have these positions filled by?
Of course, we could do that.
Okay and uhm, lastly on this topic, why does the amount of city funding increase from year to year?
Uhm, do you mean - I’m sorry, I’m not sure, you mean new need itself?
Yes, for -

Oh, uhm, it’s just simply to reflect the fact that city funding had not been appropriately budgeted in the outyears in previous

budgets. So, the dollar amount is increasing simply just to match our spending.

Okay. Uhm, and then street homeless services new need. The Preliminary Plan included additional city funding to DHS’s budget for street homeless services totaling $9.7 million in Fiscal 2026, $31.2 million in Fiscal ‘27, $29.9 million in Fiscal ‘28, $30.8 million in Fiscal ‘29, and $31.7 million in Fiscal 2030. There were also 66 additional baselined positions added. What is this additional funding for and how was the amount determined?
